meta.title: Can Trust in Science Be Improved? An Adaptive Experiment Testing Student-Designed Messages

exploratory.title: Robustness to finishers-only sample
exploratory.rationale: Respondents who did not finish the survey may differ in ways that could shift the planned estimates, so the planned model is re-fit on completers only.
exploratory.method: The planned model for trust in science is re-estimated on respondents who finished the survey and compared arm by arm with the original estimates, which used the full sample.
exploratory.finding: The finishers-only sample is the same 7,803 respondents as the main model (every analysed respondent finished the survey), so the estimates and standard errors are identical and 5 of 32 arms are significant at p<0.05 in both. The check cannot test sensitivity to partial completion.

exploratory.title: Heterogeneity by the gender column
exploratory.rationale: Gender is an available demographic not registered as a moderator, so a check on whether arm effects differ by it helps interpret the planned average effects.
exploratory.method: The planned model is extended with an interaction between each arm and a 0/1 gender indicator, giving the difference in each arm's effect between the two gender groups.
exploratory.finding: Five of 32 arm-by-gender interactions are significant at p<0.05 without correction, more than the roughly 1.6 expected by chance alone; with no correction for 32 tests, treat them as leads, not findings.

exploratory.title: Component item post_science_1 as outcome
exploratory.rationale: Examining one component item of the trust outcome shows whether the planned effects are driven by a specific belief about science.
exploratory.method: The planned model is re-fit with a single post-test science belief item as the outcome, comparing each message arm with the control group.
exploratory.finding: Two of 32 arm estimates are significant at p<0.05 on the post_science_1 item, with an average arm estimate near zero (0.004).

lit.text: The retrieved set contains little work that speaks directly to the study's hypothesis, which concerns the effect of 32 distinct messages on trust in science relative to a pure control. The closest material concerns how interventions and trials are described and reported, as in the TIDieR checklist, which argues that incomplete intervention descriptions hinder replication and implementation (Hoffmann et al., 2014), and the SPIRIT 2013 guidance on trial protocol completeness (Chan et al., 2013). These works address reporting standards rather than the effects of messages on trust, so they bear on how the 32 message conditions should be specified and documented rather than on the direction or size of any effect. No retrieved work reports an effect of science-related messaging on trust in science, so the search offers no finding that clearly agrees or disagrees with an expected effect. The remaining on-topic items are methodological: CONSORT's pilot-and-feasibility extension (Eldridge et al., 2016) and the CFIR update (Damschroder et al., 2022) concern trial reporting and implementation context. The study's design, a multi-arm randomised comparison against a single control, can speak to the reporting concerns these works raise, but the retrieved set does not establish a live empirical dispute about messaging effects.

takeaways: Across 32 messages, few moved trust in science, and effects were small: five arms differed from control on the 5-point trust scale, two of them lowering trust and three raising it.
The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust in science by 0.17 scale points (95% CI [−0.26, −0.08], p < 0.001) in the registered test.
Three untitled or student-made videos raised trust in science by about 0.06 points each, with intervals close to zero, and the 'Powers of Ten' film lowered it by 0.10.
Caveat: 32 uncorrected two-sided tests were run, several arms are small, and the borderline results should be read cautiously.
sections.abstract: Can short messages raise trust in science? This registered adaptive survey experiment randomly assigned US adults recruited through Lucid to a pure control or one of 32 messages, including videos, texts, images and memes, many made by students. The outcome was trust in science after treatment, measured on a five-point scale. Of the 11,519 respondents, 8,572 were analysed. Five arms differed from control. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.17 points (95% CI [−0.26, −0.08], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' film lowered it by 0.10 (95% CI [−0.18, −0.02], p = 0.010). Three videos raised it by about 0.06 points each, with intervals that approach zero. For the other arms no difference was detected. Because 32 tests were left uncorrected and several arms are small, the positive findings in particular are tentative.
sections.design_notes: The study was registered on OSF, with later amendments covering the assignment algorithm and covariate adjustment. Of 11,519 raw respondents, 8,572 entered the analysis; the models used 7,803 rows after missing values were dropped. Respondents were US adults from Lucid. Each of 32 messages was compared with the pure control, whose mean trust was 3.69. Arm sizes vary widely because assignment was adaptive, from about 116 to over 900 per arm. P-values are two-sided and uncorrected.

results.H1: Five of the 32 messages were distinguishable from control. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.17 points (95% CI [−0.26, −0.08], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' film by 0.10 (95% CI [−0.18, −0.02], p = 0.010). Student-made video 20 raised trust by 0.06 (95% CI [0.016, 0.111], p = 0.009), as did video 15 (95% CI [0.014, 0.112], p = 0.012) and video 12 (95% CI [0.005, 0.123], p = 0.034). For the other 27 arms no difference was detected, though the intervals are wide. With 32 uncorrected tests, the weaker results may be chance.

exploratory.E1: Exploratory and unreviewed: the finishers-only model used the same 7,803 rows as the original model, with identical estimates. The check is therefore uninformative and adds no robustness evidence.
exploratory.E2: Exploratory and unreviewed: 5 of 32 arm-by-gender interactions had p < 0.05 without correction, more than the roughly 1.6 expected by chance. Given the number of uncorrected tests, this is weak evidence that effects differed by gender.
exploratory.E3: Exploratory and unreviewed: using a single trust item as the outcome, only one visible arm (Video 12) had p < 0.05. The counts and average across all arms are not verified in the shown table. It offers little support for the registered pattern.

sections.limitations: Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without multiplicity correction, so some of the five significant arms may be false positives; the three positive effects are small and their intervals nearly reach zero. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. Several student videos have no recorded title, which limits interpreting what drove their effects. The sample is a Lucid online panel of US adults and may not generalise. Trust was measured right after exposure, so durability is unknown. The exploratory checks come from unreviewed code.

extensions.title: Decomposing the 'trust science too much' backfire
extensions.why: Addresses the design and power causes: it replaces bundled stimuli with a manipulated mechanism and concentrates sample on the one robust effect.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of -0.17 for the video; the pooled SD implied by the SEs is about 0.9. The ~0.12 MDE allows for shrinkage of the original estimate, and the power table gives no contrasts.

extensions.rationale: In the source study the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.17 points (SE 0.046, p<0.001), but it bundles fallibility framing, video format and a particular source (vlogbrothers). Other arms were small (about 120 respondents in some), so the cause of the drop cannot be isolated. This design manipulates each feature directly and adds a one-week re-measure.
extensions.contribution: Identifies whether fallibility content, video format or source drives the one robust negative effect on trust in science, and whether it persists.
extensions.hypothesis: The original video lowers trust relative to control, and the drop is mainly due to the fallibility segment: the no-fallibility video and the neutral video will not lower trust, and the transcript will lower trust by a similar amount to the video.
extensions.primary_outcome: Post-treatment trust in science: mean of the 6-item scale (items 4-6 reverse-coded), 5-point.
extensions.comparison: Each arm versus pure control, adjusting for pre-treatment trust; original video versus no-fallibility video (fallibility effect); original video versus transcript (format effect); no-fallibility video versus neutral video (source/other content); one-week outcome analysed the same way.
unresolved: Actual video files, edited no-fallibility cut, transcript and neutral video must be supplied by the research team.
Delayed one-week follow-up wave must be fielded separately; its instrument repeats the post-trust items.

power_target.basis: Observed +0.06 effects for videos 12, 15 and 20, with SD about 0.9; 80% power at alpha 0.05 needs roughly 3,500-4,400 per arm. A single contrast is not computed in the power table.

extensions.rationale: Videos 12, 15 and 20 raised trust by about 0.06 (Video 12 CI [0.005, 0.123]; Video 15 CI [0.014, 0.112]) among 32 uncorrected tests, with intervals near zero. A confirmatory replication in a new panel with few tests, plus moderation by baseline trust and party, tests whether the effects are real and where they hold.
extensions.contribution: Provides a pre-registered, multiplicity-limited replication of three small positive video effects in a non-Lucid sample and tests moderation by baseline trust and party.
extensions.hypothesis: Videos 12, 15 and 20 each raise post-treatment trust in science relative to control by about 0.06 points; effects differ by baseline trust (low vs high) and party identification.

results.H1: Five of the 32 messages were distinguishable from control. The 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowered trust by 0.17 points (95% CI [−0.26, −0.08], p < 0.001), and the 'Powers of Ten' film by 0.10 (95% CI [−0.18, −0.02], p = 0.010). exploratory.E1: Exploratory and unreviewed: restricting to respondents who finished the survey left five arms significant, the same count as the full sample, with unchanged standard errors. This agrees with the registered estimates.
exploratory.E2: Exploratory and unreviewed: five of 32 arm-by-gender interactions were significant without correction, about what chance would produce. This gives no clear evidence that effects differed by gender.
exploratory.E3: Exploratory and unreviewed: using a single trust item as the outcome, two of 32 arms were significant and the average arm estimate was near zero (0.004). It offers little support for the registered pattern.

sections_draft.limitations: Thirty-two two-sided tests were run without multiplicity correction, so some of the five significant arms may be false positives; the three positive effects are small and their intervals nearly reach zero. Adaptive assignment left some arms with only about 120 respondents, giving wide intervals. Several student videos have no recorded title, which limits interpreting what drove their effects. The sample is a Lucid online panel of US adults and may not generalise. Trust was measured right after exposure, so durability is unknown. The exploratory checks come from unreviewed code.

got_right: Pre-registered with documented amendments (assignment algorithm, Lin covariate adjustment), so the 32-arm comparison against one control is confirmatory, not post hoc.
Unusually broad stimulus set (videos, text, images, memes, many student-made) tested in one pool with a shared control (mean trust 3.69, n=664), which allows direct comparison of message formats.
Lin-adjusted, inverse-probability-weighted models with HC2 errors respect the adaptive assignment and gain precision from pre-treatment trust.

The strongest result, the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video lowering trust by 0.17 (95% CI [-0.26,-0.08], p=0.0002), is a clear backfire signal that survives scrutiny better than the small positives.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Adaptive assignment left most arms near 120-180 respondents, so per-arm intervals are about ±0.15 and cannot detect effects of the size seen (0.06). Three of the five 'significant' arms are small positives whose intervals almost reach zero.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Arm n of 116-180 for most arms versus 853-921 for videos 15 and 20; Video 12 CI [0.005, 0.123], p=0.034.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Thirty-two uncorrected two-sided tests were run. Only the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video clearly survives a Bonferroni threshold (0.05/32≈0.0016). The other four, p of 0.009 to 0.034, are consistent with chance.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Five of 32 arms at p<0.05 against about 1.6 expected under the null; p=0.0002, 0.0093, 0.0104, 0.0116, 0.0341.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Each arm bundles content, format, length and source, and several student videos have no recorded title. Even a real effect cannot be attributed to any feature of the message.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Video 12, Video 15 and Student-made video (20) are untitled or minimally described uploads.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Trust is measured once, immediately after exposure, on a 5-point scale, and the single-item check shows almost no signal. The effects are small relative to the scale and durability is unknown.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Control mean 3.685; positive effects about 0.06; the single-item outcome has only one visible arm (Video 12, p=0.048).

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The pipeline's completers robustness check reused the same 7,803 rows as the main model, so it supplies no robustness evidence. Modelling used 7,803 of 8,572 analysed rows.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: E1 shows orig_n = compl_n = 7803 with identical estimates; the checking agent's correction says the same.

briefs.title: Decomposing the 'trust science too much' backfire
briefs.question: Which feature of the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video (its fallibility framing, its format, or its source) lowers trust in science?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the design and power causes: it replaces bundled stimuli with a manipulated mechanism and concentrates sample on the one robust effect.
briefs.design_sketch: Randomise respondents to the original video, a text transcript of it, a version without the fallibility segment, a matched-length neutral video, and a pure control. Outcome is the same 5-point trust measure, with pre-treatment trust as a covariate and a delayed re-measure after about one week. Sample is US adults from an online panel, with the same exclusions as the original.

power_target.basis: Observed effect of -0.17 for the video; the pooled SD implied by the SEs is about 0.9. The ~0.12 MDE allows for shrinkage of the original estimate, and the power table gives no contrasts.

briefs.title: Do the small positive videos replicate across samples and baseline trust?
briefs.question: Do the three small positive video effects (about +0.06) replicate in a fresh sample, and do they differ by baseline trust or partisanship?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the multiplicity and sample causes: a confirmatory replication of the three positive arms with a single correction, plus a test of where the effect holds.
briefs.design_sketch: Run videos 12, 15 and 20, the strongest-effect comparison video, and a control in a new panel, preferably a different vendor from Lucid. Pre-register three directional tests, with the interaction of arm and pre-treatment trust (low versus high) and of arm and party identification. Add a title and a content coding for each student video so features can be linked to effects.
briefs.moderator_or_condition: Baseline trust in science (low vs high) and party identification, across a different panel vendor.

power_target.basis: Observed +0.06 effects for videos 12, 15 and 20, with SD about 0.9; 80% power at alpha 0.05 needs roughly 3,500-4,400 per arm. A single contrast is not computed in the power table.

briefs.title: Archive stimuli and arm-level assignment data
briefs.question: Can the untitled student videos and the adaptive assignment log be documented well enough to attribute effects to content?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses the measurement and design causes: untitled stimuli cannot be interpreted or replicated.
briefs.design_sketch: Recover the files for videos 8, 10, 12, 15, 25 and 32. Have two coders rate each on length, tone, presence of an expert, and fallibility framing, using the TIDieR checklist. Publish the assignment probabilities by wave so inverse-probability weights can be audited.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but narrowly. Only the 'Can You Trust Science Too Much?' video backfire (-0.17, p=0.0002) is robust to multiplicity. The three +0.06 effects are fragile, and the pipeline's completers check added no evidence. The retrieved literature is reporting-standards material, so no live empirical debate is visible and none is invented. Run the backfire decomposition first, since it has the largest effect and an explicit mechanism. Then run the larger replication of the positive videos, with stimulus documentation (the data brief) done in parallel at little cost.
